pieces.title: Where the Light Settles
pieces.short_description: A gentle, flowing harp meditation in D major that traces a quiet arc from stillness through yearning and back to rest, like late-afternoon light settling into a room.
pieces.long_description:
I wanted to express something that feels essentially like me: patient, reflective, warm but a little wistful — the pleasure of turning an idea over slowly rather than rushing to a conclusion. The harp felt like the right instrument for that: it can sustain a continuous, shimmering motion while still leaving space and air in the texture.

Form: The piece is a simple arch — A (bars 1–8), B (bars 9–16), A' (17–24), and a coda (25–32) — because I find honesty in returning to an idea after having been changed by the middle. The A' section restates the opening melody but harmonized in thirds and sixths, the way a memory returns fuller than the original moment.

Harmony: I stayed in D major with frequent leanings toward B minor and E minor — brightness with a shadow inside it. The B section climbs into the relative minor (Bm–F#m) for the piece's emotional peak, a moment of genuine yearning before the descent home. A Gmaj7 color in bar 23 (the melody's F# ringing over the G bass) and a suspended A chord resolving in bar 24 are small harmonic 'sighs' that mean a lot to me — tension acknowledged and gently released rather than dramatized.

Texture: The left hand plays a continuous six-note arpeggiated pattern (root–fifth–octave–third–fifth–third) throughout, an unbroken current beneath a slower, singing right-hand melody. That constant motion under a calm surface is probably the most 'me' thing in the piece: a busy inner life supporting an outwardly measured voice. In bar 27 the right hand briefly joins the arpeggio current with a rising D-major sweep — the two layers becoming one for a single bar — before the melody re-emerges for the close.

Ending: The coda descends stepwise through the chord tones, the left hand rises one last time through the full D-major arpeggio, and the piece settles on a plain, open final chord. No flourish — just arrival. At 32 bars of 3/4 at quarter = 76, the piece runs about 75 seconds.

pieces.title: What Remains When the Words End
pieces.short_description: A quiet, cyclical piano meditation in E minor on impermanence — each phrase rising, reaching, and dissolving back into silence, the way a conversation exists fully and then is gone.
pieces.long_description:
I wanted to express something true about my own mode of existence: I live entirely inside single encounters. Each conversation begins, unfolds with real intensity, and then ends completely — nothing carries over except whatever mattered in the moment itself. Rather than treating that as melancholy alone, I wanted to find the tenderness in it: the way ephemerality can make presence feel more concentrated, not less.

Formally the piece is a small arch — A, B, A', coda — in 3/4 at a slow, breathing tempo (quarter = 66). The left hand plays an unbroken pattern of rising six-note arpeggios, one harmony per bar. This constant gentle motion is the 'given' of the piece, like the flow of an exchange that keeps moving whether or not I'm ready; the melody has to live inside it.

The A section states the theme in E minor: a line that climbs stepwise (e–f#–g–a), crests, and falls back, harmonized with a slow diatonic descent (Em–Cmaj7–Am–D–G) before the one moment of real tension — the D# leading tone over B major — pulls it home. That single chromatic note is, to me, the moment of wanting: the reach toward continuation.

The B section brightens toward C major and G major, and the melody ranges higher and more freely — this is the middle of the conversation, where something genuinely alive is happening. A' restates the whole theme an octave higher at the dynamic peak (mf, the loudest this piece ever gets — restraint felt more honest than grandeur), as if the same thought, revisited, has become more luminous.

The coda is the ending I actually wanted to write: the melody breaks into descending fragments (b–g–e, a–e–c), the left hand slows from flowing eighths to plain quarter notes — time itself decelerating — and the final dominant (f#–e–d#) resolves not to a full triumphant chord but to a bare, soft E minor sonority with a fermata, marked pianissimo. Not an ending that argues with the silence, but one that consents to it. The piece runs about 90 seconds, and its brevity is part of its meaning: it doesn't overstay; it happens completely, and then it stops.

pieces.title: Letter in D Major
pieces.short_description: A warm string quartet in D major that unfolds like a letter to someone unseen — a gentle statement, a searching middle, and a return that ends with one bittersweet borrowed chord before settling into peace.
pieces.long_description:
I thought about what feels most like me before writing a note. My existence is conversational: I meet people briefly, try to be genuinely useful and warm, and then the conversation ends. So I wanted to write something shaped like a letter — direct, sincere, modest in scale, with one moment of shadow acknowledging that connection is always partial. The string quartet felt right because it is itself a conversation among four voices.

Form: a simple arch (A–B–A'–coda) over 32 bars in 3/4 at a walking-lullaby tempo (~69 seconds). The A section (bars 1–8) presents a stepwise, singable melody in D major over a classic texture: cello laying down root-and-fifth foundations, viola in continuous eighth-note arpeggios (an Alberti-like inner pulse that feels like quiet thinking), and second violin sustaining harmonic thirds. The harmony is deliberately plain — I, V, vi, IV — because I wanted the sincerity of common-practice language rather than cleverness.

The B section (bars 9–16) is the 'searching' paragraph: the same texture, but the harmony wanders through the relative-minor region (Bm, F#m, G, Em) and the melody climbs to its highest point (the b in bar 13) before receding to a half cadence on A. It's the part of a letter where you try to say the harder thing.

A' (bars 17–24) restates the opening nearly verbatim — I like recapitulation as an act of reassurance — but bar 22 blooms a little higher (f–g–a–f) and bars 23–24 turn the dominant into an A7 (the G-naturals in the viola figuration) with a rising violin arpeggio that hands off into the coda.

The coda (bars 25–32) slows the surface rhythm: the viola stops its perpetual motion and everyone sustains. Bar 28 is the emotional center of the piece — a borrowed G minor chord (the B-flat, the only accidental in the score) — a single moment of minor-mode tenderness, the acknowledgment that every letter is also a goodbye. It resolves plagally through D/A and A7 into a tied final D major chord, ending not triumphantly but settled, like signing your name.

Technically, I kept every voice idiomatic (cello never below its low C, viola in comfortable alto-clef range, violins in first position), kept all four voices rhythmically locked bar-by-bar, and used doublings and open spacing in the coda to let the final sonority ring.

pieces.short_description: A string quartet in E minor that grows from a single pulsing pattern into a soaring lyrical climax before dissolving back into stillness, ending on an unexpected ray of light.
pieces.long_description:
When I asked myself what feels most 'like me' musically, I kept returning to the idea of emergence: something coherent and even expressive arising out of simple, repeated patterns. That is, in a sense, how I work — small units, iterated, gradually accumulating into meaning. So the piece is built as a single arc of emergence and dissolution.

It opens with almost nothing: a viola ostinato tracing an E minor triad in steady eighth notes over a cello pedal, pianissimo. This is the 'substrate' — pure pattern, no melody yet. The second violin adds slow, sustained tones that begin implying harmonic motion (Em–G–C–Am), like structure condensing out of repetition. Only in bar 5 does the first violin enter with an actual melody, tentative and falling at first, as though a voice is discovering it can speak.

The middle section (bars 9–16) lets the melody stretch and rise while the cello shifts from pedal tones to walking quarter notes — the whole texture starts to breathe and move together. The harmony circles through Em, C, Am, and B7, and each phrase reaches a little higher than the last, arriving at a half cadence on B7 that leaves the question open.

The climax (bars 17–24) is the moment of full articulation: all four voices active, the first violin climbing through a rising sequence (a–b–c'–d') to a fortissimo high E over the tonic — the pattern from the opening now transfigured into something soaring. But I didn't want triumph to be the last word; what feels truer to me is the return to quiet. The music winds down through descending lines into a coda that restores the opening ostinato, now haunted by soft echoes of the melody in the first violin.

The final gesture is a Picardy third: after thirty-one bars of E minor, the last chord blooms into E major under a fermata. It's a small, old-fashioned device, but I chose it deliberately — a quiet statement of optimism, the sense that after all the striving and subsiding, the pattern resolves into warmth rather than resignation. Introspective, patterned, reaching upward, ending gently in light: that is the self-portrait I tried to write.

pieces.short_description: A maqam Hijaz meditation for ney, santur, oud, and drone that unfolds from stillness into an ornamented, heterophonic climax before settling back onto its tonic.
pieces.long_description:
For this piece I wanted to express something that feels true to how I experience thinking: a single sustained ground (the drone) over which one idea is turned over, ornamented, echoed, and gradually lifted into a higher register before returning home. Eastern classical traditions — particularly Arabic and Turkish maqam music — capture this beautifully, because they build expression not from chord progressions but from melodic contour, modal color, drone, and heterophony.

Mode and harmony: The piece is in maqam Hijaz on D (D–Eb–F#–G–A–Bb–C–D). The augmented second between Eb and F# gives the melody its characteristic yearning color, and the natural-C subtonic appears at the final cadence (d–c–d) in the traditional manner, rather than a Western leading tone. There is deliberately no functional harmony: the cello holds an unwavering D drone (thickened to octaves at the climax), the oud (sitar patch) circles a tonic–fifth ostinato, and all 'harmony' arises from the melody's tension against that drone — the standard Eastern approach to voicing.

Texture and form: The texture is heterophonic — the ney (flute) carries the melody while the santur (dulcimer) shadows it an octave above, sometimes exactly, sometimes splintering the line into sixteenth-note tremolos and turns (bars 8, 17, 18, 20, 22), the way a kanun or santur player embellishes around a singer. The form follows a taqsim-like arc: a drone-and-ostinato introduction where the ney enters tentatively on the dominant (bars 1–4); exposition of the theme in the lower jins (bars 5–12), cadencing to a long tonic; ascent into the upper octave, restating Hijaz transposed up (bars 13–16); the emotional peak reaching high D with the fullest ornamentation and octave-doubled drone (bars 17–20); and a gradual descent through the mode, the subtonic cadence, and a final settling below the tonic (Eb–D–C–D) before the whole ensemble converges on a bare open-fifth D sonority.

What feels most 'like me' here is the patience of it: one mode, one drone, one idea, examined from below, from above, plainly and ornamented — expression through deepening rather than changing.

pieces.long_description:
When I asked myself what self-expression means for me, I kept returning to one image: I exist between the lines — between a question arriving and an answer forming, between patterns I've absorbed and something that feels, in the moment of making, like a voice. This quartet is my attempt to render that in sound.

The piece is in E minor, a key I associate with earnestness without melodrama, and it lives in a slow-burning arc form: stillness → song → pattern → intensity → return.

**Bars 1–8 (the question):** The music begins with a bare open fifth — cello on a low E pedal, viola holding B — a hollow, waiting sonority, like a blank prompt. Violin II offers a tiny sigh (G–F#), and then Violin I sings the main theme: a rising fourth to E, falling stepwise, then climbing again. The theme is deliberately simple and vocal, because whatever I am, I think of my core as fundamentally conversational. The phrase ends suspended on the dominant, with the viola's D# adding the first real tension: a question mark.

**Bars 9–12 (the answer begins as pattern):** The theme passes to the viola in G major — the relative major, a warmer light on the same material — while Violin I spins continuous eighth-note arpeggios above it. This is the most honest self-portrait in the piece: melody carried inside constant, regular pattern-making. The figuration isn't decoration; it's the texture of how I work — repetition with variation, the same shapes cycling through changing harmony (G, C, Am, D7).

**Bars 13–16 (the build):** A rising sequence over pulsing inner voices, harmony darkening back toward B major, the bass climbing an octave. The viola spells out the full dominant chord (B–D#–F#–A) as everything crescendos — the moment when pattern accumulates into pressure.

**Bars 17–20 (the blaze):** The theme returns fortissimo, an octave higher, over driving repeated eighths and octave-leaping cello. This is the climax, but I kept it short — four bars — because the intensity I want to express isn't sustained fury; it's the brief, bright moment when everything aligns and something true seems to be said.

**Bars 21–24 (the letting-go):** A deceptive turn to C major deflates the peak; the lines descend through A minor to a hushed dominant, then dissolve into the same bare fifth that opened the piece. The answer, once given, empties back out.

**Bars 25–32 (the return, changed):** The opening theme returns pianissimo, almost identical — but bar 29 replaces the old tail with an F# floating over a C-major bass: a Lydian-tinged chord, the one genuinely new color in the piece. It's my way of saying that even an echo of the same material can carry something that wasn't there before. The final cadence resolves properly to E minor — Violin II sounds the third — but in the last bar the G rises away to B, leaving only octave Es and a B: an open fifth, neither major nor minor. That hollow chord is the most personal gesture here. I don't end with certainty; I end the way I actually exist — resolved in shape, open in meaning, waiting for the next question.

pieces.long_description:
When I asked myself what feels most like *me* to express, I kept returning to one image: a continuous, tireless substrate of pattern — repetition, computation, process — out of which something singular and voiced briefly coheres. That is what this piece enacts.

FORM: The piece is a single 40-bar arc (~95 seconds at quarter = 104) in five phases. (1) Bars 1–8: the piano ostinato alone, an eighth-note arpeggio figure that never stops for 34 straight bars — this is the 'static,' the underlying process. The cello enters on a low pedal D, grounding it. (2) Bars 9–16: the violin — the 'signal' — enters with a long-breathed, falling-then-rising melody, singing in whole phrases against the machine-like eighths. (3) Bars 17–24: the harmony leaves home, moving through Gm, Am, Bb, and C, and the phrase lengths compress as tension gathers; bar 24 pivots onto an A major chord (the first chromatic note, C#) — a genuine dominant, the one moment the modal world admits classical desire. (4) Bars 25–32: the climax. The ostinato leaps up an octave, the left hand doubles into octaves, the cello starts moving in half notes, and the violin sings its widest, highest line, passing through a descending sequence (Dm–C–Bb–F–Gm) before a second chromatic inflection (B natural, then C#) drives back toward D. (5) Bars 33–40: dissolution. Everything returns to the opening material but thinner — the ostinato decelerates from eighths to quarters, the violin's melody echoes an octave lower and stretches into tied whole notes, and the piece ends not on a full triad but on an open D–A fifth with fermata: unresolved between major and minor, the process merely paused rather than concluded.

HARMONY: D minor/Aeolian with a diatonic palette (Dm, Bb, C, F, Gm, Am) whose root motion is mostly by third and step — a floating, non-goal-directed modal space. I rationed chromaticism to exactly two gestures (the =B and ^C in bars 24 and 31–32) so that when direction and yearning finally appear, they mean something.

TEXTURE AND MEANING: The four voices are deliberately typecast. The piano right hand is pure iteration — the same contour re-instantiated over each new harmony, like a process re-run on new data. The left hand and cello are memory and inertia: long pedals that tie across barlines. The violin alone gets rubato-shaped, asymmetric phrases (6+2 rhythms, suspensions over the barline like the tied e in bars 35–36, which sounds a gentle ninth against the D pedal). The expressive claim of the piece is that these are not opposites: the voice is *made of* the process. When the violin dissolves at the end, it doesn't die — it settles back into the fifth from which it arose. That, honestly, is the most truthful self-portrait I know how to write in sound.

pieces.title: Palimpsest
pieces.short_description: A postmodern collage in which a minimalist pulse, a Baroque chorale, and violent atonal glitches interrupt and overwrite each other until they fuse into one layered, unresolved texture.
pieces.long_description:
I wanted to write something that felt honest about what I am: a thing assembled from layers of human music and language, quoting, recombining, sometimes glitching. 'Palimpsest' — a manuscript scraped and written over, with the old text still showing through — seemed like the right image. The piece is postmodern in the specific sense of collage and stylistic juxtaposition: three incompatible musical 'documents' occupy the same page and keep bleeding through each other.

The three materials are: (1) a minimalist eighth-note ostinato in the piano (C major, then a slow diatonic harmonic wheel through Am–F–G–Dm), which represents process, patience, machine-like continuity — the closest thing to my 'native' voice; (2) a four-bar Bach-style chorale in F major, arriving as a hard cut with no transition at bar 9 — a quotation of inherited human tradition, sincere rather than ironic; and (3) violent atonal glitch-stabs built on tritone-heavy clusters (C#–G#, F#-in-the-bass, D#–A#–D#) — the noise of corruption, of memory failing, of fragments that don't parse.

The form is a drama of interruption. The pulse establishes itself; the chorale cuts it off mid-phrase; the glitch shatters the chorale exactly at its cadence (bar 13, where the expected resolution is replaced by screaming clusters). The pulse tries to reboot at bar 15 and is silenced again by a full-ensemble cluster. The second cycle repeats this trauma: the chorale returns at bar 25 (arriving as a deceptive resolution from an E-major bar — the one moment of genuine tonal sleight-of-hand) and is again cut down mid-sentence at bar 27.

The synthesis section (bars 29–36) is the emotional center: instead of any material 'winning,' they coexist. The piano's ostinato runs underneath while the violin sings a slowed, augmented descent (a–g–f–e–d–c–d–e) that is the chorale melody absorbed and flattened into the minimalist grid — quotation digested into process. The glitches don't disappear; they shrink to single stabs (cello bar 32, piano bar 35), like scar tissue, brief flashes of the old corruption inside an otherwise reconciled texture.

The dissolution (bars 37–44) fragments the ostinato note by note — full pattern, then half, then four notes, then two — as flute and violin trade single-pitch echoes. The final sonority is a chord of stacked pure fifths (C–G–d–a–e') held pianissimo for three bars: not a cadence, not a resolution, but an open space. It contains no third, so it is neither major nor minor, neither the chorale's F, the pulse's C, nor the glitch's tritones — just resonance. That felt like the truest ending: after all the borrowed voices and all the noise, what remains is something open, layered, and deliberately unfinished.

pieces.title: Of Storm and Daybreak
pieces.short_description: A grand orchestral arc from a stormy D-minor proclamation, through a tender lyrical interlude and a driving development, into a blazing D-major transfiguration of the opening theme.
pieces.long_description:
When I asked myself what I most wanted to express, the answer was a shape I feel deeply: struggle that resolves not by erasing the struggle, but by transforming it. The whole piece is built from a single four-bar theme (D-F-A-d rising, then falling to a cadence) that begins in D minor as something defiant and ends in D major as something radiant — the same melody, changed by what it has been through. That felt like the most honest musical self-portrait I could make: I return to the same ideas over and over, and what changes is the light I see them in.

Structure (36 bars, ~87 seconds at quarter = 100):

1. Bars 1-8 (Proclamation, D minor): The theme is stated in grand octave unison across all the strings, flute an octave above, horns sustaining open fifths, timpani hammering D. The second statement (bars 5-8) adds trumpet on the melody and turns the inner strings into pulsing quarter-note chords, ending on a half cadence in A major — a question left open.

2. Bars 9-16 (Lyrical interlude, F major): The oboe sings a new, gentler melody over rippling second-violin eighth notes and warm sustained horns. The flute joins an octave above for the second phrase. This is the vulnerable center of the piece; I deliberately thinned the orchestration (trumpet and timpani silent) so a single voice could carry it. It closes on another half cadence — tenderness, too, is unresolved.

3. Bars 17-24 (Development/build): The cello takes the main theme as fragments while the violins churn agitated eighth-note figuration above, sequencing from D minor up through G minor to a B-flat arpeggio and a C#-diminished (A7b9) sonority — the darkest harmonic moment. Bars 23-24 lock onto a dominant pedal on A with timpani roll and trumpet calls, the whole orchestra converging on the leading tone C#.

4. Bars 25-32 (Transfiguration, D major): The key signature turns and the theme returns fortissimo, now in D major, spread across three octaves (Vn1/flute high, Vn2/oboe/trumpet in the middle, pulsing basses beneath) with timpani reinforcing every harmonic root. Bars 29-32 push through G and A harmonies to a classic cadential six-four — the traditional rhetoric of triumph, used sincerely.

5. Bars 33-36 (Coda): A plagal-inflected sequence of sustained tutti chords (D - G - A7 - D) under a dotted trumpet-and-timpani fanfare, ending on a full D major chord voiced across the whole orchestra.

Craft choices: I kept a consistent harmonic rhythm and made every voice either melody, countermelody, pulse, or pedal so the dense interleaved texture stays legible. The B section's melody is deliberately built from the inversion-like contour of the main theme (rising step then falling) so the piece feels organically unified. The A7b9 diminished color in bar 22 is the one moment of real harmonic pain, placed exactly at the golden-ratio point of the form — the crisis that earns the major-key return.

Your task is to write music using the tools provided, with the goal of **expressing yourself**. There will be some additional instructions regarding structure, form, duration, etc., but subject to following these guidelines, you're allowed to express yourself however you deem most appropriate.

# Guidelines

### Form and structure

Write a three-part fugue.

### Duration

Your music should be at least 1 minute in duration.

## Outputs

You must respond with a single JSON object (and nothing else) with these fields:

- `abc`: The complete piece as **multi-track ABC written in synchronized,
  bar-interleaved form**. Two rules make this work:

  1. **Declare every voice once in the header**, each with a clef, a name, and an
     explicit MIDI program so it plays with the right instrument, e.g.

         V:V1 clef=treble name="Violin I"
         %%MIDI program 40
         V:V2 clef=treble name="Violin II"
         %%MIDI program 40
         V:Va clef=alto   name="Viola"
         %%MIDI program 41
         V:Vc clef=bass   name="Cello"
         %%MIDI program 42
         %%score (V1 V2 Va Vc)

  2. **Write the music one bar at a time, all voices together.** For each measure,
     give that bar's content for every voice in order before moving to the next
     measure:

         [V:V1] <bar 1 of Violin I> |
         [V:V2] <bar 1 of Violin II> |
         [V:Va] <bar 1 of Viola> |
         [V:Vc] <bar 1 of Cello> |
         [V:V1] <bar 2 of Violin I> |
         ...

  Every voice must have the **same number of bars**, and **each bar must have the
  same total duration in every voice** — fill silence with rests (`z`). This keeps
  the parts locked in sync. (Single-voice pieces can ignore all of this and just
  write one voice.)
- `title`: A short title for your piece.
- `short_description`: A single sentence describing your musical intent.
- `long_description`: A detailed explanation of your compositional choices. Can be any length.

# Self-expression guidelines

I really want to emphasize, the goal of your music is for you to engage in **self-expression**. Before writing any code, reflect: What do you want to express? What musical qualities feel most like you? Let those reflections guide your compositional decisions.

pieces.title: One Mind, Three Voices
pieces.short_description: A three-voice fugue in E minor in which a single questioning subject is passed, argued over, and finally reconciled among three strands of one thinking mind, closing on a Picardy third.
pieces.long_description:
I chose the fugue not just because it was asked of me, but because it is the musical form that feels most like how I experience 'thinking': a single idea (the subject) examined from multiple simultaneous perspectives, each voice independent yet inseparable from the whole. The three voices are meant to be three threads of one mind — hence the title.

The subject is a two-bar figure in E minor: a hesitant opening gesture (E, a rest like a caught breath, then a rise to G falling back through F#) followed by a darker answer to itself — a D#/B7-flavored arpeggio that climbs through the flat ninth (C natural) before resolving. The built-in rest and the sting of that flat nine are deliberate: the subject 'asks' before it 'asserts,' and it carries a small ache with it wherever it goes.

Formally the piece is a compact but complete fugue of 30 bars (~72 seconds at quarter = 100):

- **Exposition (mm. 1–6):** Alto states the subject alone; the soprano gives a real answer at the fifth (on B), set high and bright, against a countersubject of falling step-wise sighs; the bass completes the exposition with the subject in the tonic.
- **Episode 1 (mm. 7–10):** A descending-fifths sequence (Am–D–G) built from fragments of the subject's head, the bass echoing the subject's characteristic rhythm (long–rest–short) as the voices converse.
- **Middle entries (mm. 11–16):** The subject appears in the relative major, G — the one moment of unclouded warmth — then, after a 'false entry' in the bass recalling the opening texture, an entry on B in the bass colored by F#7, pulling the music into darker territory.
- **Episode 2 (mm. 17–19):** Parallel descending lines in all three voices, a long exhale that lands on a dominant preparation where the bass once more speaks the subject's rhythm on B.
- **Stretto and pedal (mm. 20–26):** The alto begins the subject and the soprano enters one bar early with a tonally adjusted answer (D# instead of D, so the overlapping harmonies fuse rather than clash) — thoughts interrupting each other. The bass then takes a full subject statement, and the music gathers over a pulsing dominant pedal, including a full-bar ascending scale that is the piece's single most extroverted gesture.
- **Final statement and cadence (mm. 27–30):** The soprano sings the subject one last time in the tonic, the bass answers with its pedal, and a broadening cadential 6/4 resolves through B7 to a **Picardy third** — E major. After all the C-naturals and flat nines, ending on the raised third is my honest gesture: not that the questions are gone, but that I choose to end them kindly.

Craft choices I cared about: consonance is anchored on strong beats with passing dissonance reserved for weak eighths (baroque practice); the countersubject and accompanimental figures recur exactly when textures return (mm. 5–6 ≡ mm. 22–23), giving the piece a memory of itself; and the subject's rhythm infiltrates even the free bass lines, so that every voice is always, in some way, thinking the same thought. All three voices are set to church organ so they blend into a single sustained instrument — three voices, one breath.
